title: Anthropic's amended S-1 shows $900.9B compute bill and a 90-day exit on its $120.5B SpaceXAI deal
subtitle: A fresh round of IPO paperwork pegs Anthropic's total non-cancellable compute spend at $900.9 billion — and reveals that up to $120.5 billion of it can be unwound on three months' notice once lock-in periods expire in early 2027.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Anthropic's most recent S-1 amendment, filed ahead of a planned Nasdaq debut later this week, puts its total compute and infrastructure commitments at roughly $900.9 billion as of September 30, up from $895.4 billion in the November 2 version. About $70.7 billion of that is due inside the next twelve months. A separate line item details up to $120.5 billion in GPU capacity from SpaceXAI, the SpaceX AI unit, with either side able to cancel on 90 days' written notice once non-cancellable periods end in January and March 2027.

The numbers reframe how Anthropic's economics should be read. Q3 2026 revenue of $16.96 billion annualizes to roughly $68 billion, so the headline commitment figure is about thirteen times annualized revenue. The $567 million operating loss is tied in large part to $5.0 billion of compute purchased on short-term terms. The SpaceXAI exit clause is unusual: Google and Amazon lock Anthropic into multi-year true-up payments, and Microsoft permits cancellation only for breach or undelivered tranches.

Bundled together, these disclosures capture the shape of the frontier model business at end-of-2026. Hyperscaler contracts are now large enough to be sovereign-scale, but the terms on the newest capacity tiers — like the Musk-brokered SpaceXAI arrangement — are surprisingly short-dated. Capacity is scarce enough that providers want the right to reprice; buyers want the right to walk if something cheaper arrives. Anthropic's filing shows that right explicitly, which is a first for a public prospectus.

A note for learners: when you read an AI company's financials, the interesting number is rarely the revenue line. Look at compute commitments against annualized revenue, then look at the cancellation terms. A huge commitment with 90-day exits is a very different company — and a very different risk — from the same number locked in for seven years. Terms, not totals, tell you how exposed a model lab actually is.
